id: 0_B6ZDg6C5
type: theme
title: "The price of water"
---
The family’s prosperity, paid for by its children. The Combes never run short of water, even in a drought, because one child in every generation goes down. Breaking the pact means accepting a dry well (ending The Name). A theme of sacrifice handed down the generations, and of who agrees to pay in place of others ([@Marcel](cosmos:Uu1WZvJKWt), the reader in The Exchange).

title: "Dragon’s eye"
---
[@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK)’s big glass marble, with a red spiral running through it. He never lent it: “I’ll give it to you when you’re grown up.” Found in the niche in the well, among the treasures of the children who went down before (The Niche). Shown to Paul, it makes him recognise the reader.

files.cartes/5xmLViOKEx.md:
---
id: 5xmLViOKEx
type: lieu
title: "The Combes farm"
---
The family farm. Gravel yard, two-hundred-year-old walnut tree, stone trough, leaning barn, house with green shutters, workshop under a lean-to. The well at the far end of the yard, sealed since 2003 with an oak lid banded with iron and a padlock.

In the kitchen: a clock that strikes once at 3:12, a walnut bureau with a locked drawer, a photo of the two children on the rim of the well. A green door with a cat flap and a bike scrape at hip height.

To be sold before the end of the month. It has never run short of water.

files.cartes/6c01BXl0tf.md:
---
id: 6c01BXl0tf
type: personnage
title: "You (the reader)"
fiche: {"age":"33 (10 in 2003)","besoin":"To face the night of 2003"}
---
The character played by the reader, written as “you”, with no fixed gender. [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK)’s older sibling, three years older. Comes back to the Combes farm for [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s funeral, twenty-three years after their brother vanished.

**Wound:** on the night of 14 August 2003, saw Paul cross the yard towards the well and pretended to be asleep. Buried the memory (revealed in The Upside-Down Well).

**Arc:** to stop “pretending to be asleep”. The ending “The House” replays the failure; the ending “The Morning” mends it.
files.cartes/7L8ulO4BrP.md:
---
id: 7L8ulO4BrP
type: lieu
title: "The root corridor"
---
The passage between the green door at the bottom of the well and [@The farm below](cosmos:WNh9vyU3T6). Low ceiling, walls made of the roots of the walnut tree in the yard, a bitter smell of walnut husks. The roots whisper the names of the children who went down, then the reader’s, and wait for an answer. At the end, a second green door identical to the first. A threshold between the two worlds: corridor, mirror or years.
files.cartes/8290ZuJdRK.md:
---
id: 8290ZuJdRK
type: personnage
title: "Paul"
fiche: {"age":"7 (forever)"}
---
The little brother. Vanished into the well on the night of 14 August 2003, aged seven. Down there time does not pass: he is still seven, striped pyjamas, scraped knees, a cowlick, a lisp.

Counts everything (stairs, rungs, seconds): “once you have counted something, it can’t scare you any more.” Signs with a P, often backwards.

His treasure: the Dragon’s eye marble. Calls his older sibling “the other one” when he is cross.

Does not recognise the grown-up reader, except through the marble or the confession (word RECOGNISED).

title: "The Merciers"
---
The neighbours in the house at the end of the lane. In The Exchange, the reader tells Paul to go and knock at their door when he gets back up. They were probably among the “handful of neighbours” at [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s funeral.

id: Cr_QG9CABe
type: personnage
title: "Jeanne"
fiche: {"age":"A child (forever)"}
---
A Combes child who went down in 1903. Left a blue satin ribbon in the niche, carefully rolled and labelled with her name, and carved a little flower next to her name on the wall at the bottom.

Ourdas often borrows her voice: it is with hers that he announces [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s death and accepts the exchange.
files.cartes/ECm2L3EIxC.md:
---
id: ECm2L3EIxC
type: objet
title: "The 3:12 clock"
---
The kitchen clock, above the stove, stopped at twelve minutes past three. It strikes once at that hour “for no reason, and has for years”. Probably the hour [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) went down in 2003, and the hour of [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s death. In The House, something scratches at the reader’s door at 3:12.
files.cartes/FFP5HuhWqQ.md:
---
id: FFP5HuhWqQ
type: objet
title: "The lantern"
---
A paraffin lantern waiting on the workbench, already filled, matches beside it. Someone (a child?) has tried to reach it: small handprints in the dust. It can light itself if the reader sets off in the dark.

Its flame (0 to 3) is the game’s gauge: flattened by the wind in the well, damaged in the fall, worn down by the marks, refilled in the barn below. Without it, [@Ourdas](cosmos:nKFYoFi_Cw)’s name is not enough. In The Morning, it answers the name and turns white and immense.
files.cartes/G7MMg6ZoFy.md:
---
id: G7MMg6ZoFy
type: objet
title: "The rope"
---
A hemp rope coiled on the big nail in the workshop, fifteen metres, as thick as a thumb. One end cut clean, recently. The reader ties it to the pulley beam with the bowline [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie) taught for tethering calves. It saves them at the broken rung.

files.cartes/IYeVcwoIKB.md:
---
id: IYeVcwoIKB
type: theme
title: "Pretending to sleep"
---
The central theme: the guilt of not having acted, and chosen forgetting. The reader pretended to be asleep in 2003; the voice reminds them (“You’re breathing like when you pretended”). The ending The House replays the failure exactly. The confession to [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) and the ending The Morning mend it: waking up, at last. An echo in [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie), who fell asleep only once and then kept watch all her life.
files.cartes/JIEEal4oM2.md:
---
id: JIEEal4oM2
type: regle
title: "The Combes pact"
---
Struck by [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s great-grandfather during a great drought: the Combes will never run short of water; in return, in every generation, a child of the house goes down of their own accord.

Children who went down: Étienne 1874, Jeanne 1903, [@Marcel](cosmos:Uu1WZvJKWt) 1958, [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) 2003. Their names are carved by the door at the bottom (The Marks).

Broken if [@Ourdas](cosmos:nKFYoFi_Cw)’s name is spoken in front of him with light: the well dries up.
files.cartes/KaPkG8_PVU.md:

id: KaPkG8_PVU
type: secret
title: "The reader saw Paul go"
fiche: {"indices":"The Silence: the voice says “You’re breathing like when you pretended to be asleep”, and the reader has never told anyone about that. The Voice: Paul says he counted the days while he waited. The House (ending): the reader remembers hearing the door downstairs open that night and not moving. Paul: he calls his older sibling “the other one”, the name he used when he was cross.","revelation":"The Upside-Down Well: looking into the inverted well, the reader sees the night of 14 August 2003 again, and their own child’s face at the window. They can then confess it to Paul in The Confession."}
---
The reader never told anyone: on the night of 14 August 2003 they were awake, at the window, and saw their brother go to the well. They chose not to move, then to forget. Revealed in The Upside-Down Well; confessed to [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) in The Confession. Only Paul and [@Ourdas](cosmos:nKFYoFi_Cw) knew (“You breathe too loud”).
files.cartes/LQcs3WMcF6.md:
---
id: LQcs3WMcF6
type: objet
title: "The lid and the padlock"
---
An oak lid banded with iron and a padlock the size of a fist, put on by [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie) after 2003. Its inner face is scratched with hundreds of small marks: [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) counted the days on it. Odile sat on it every night (“As long as I sit on it, he can’t come up”). On the evening of the story it leans against the rim, padlock open: nobody knows who took it off.
files.cartes/OPIXlxJGtO.md:
---
id: OPIXlxJGtO
type: question
title: "Who opened the well?"
---
The lid is off, the padlock open, the lantern filled, the rope cut clean: someone prepared the descent. [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) from below? [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie) before she died, so the reader would go and fetch him? [@Ourdas](cosmos:nKFYoFi_Cw) himself? Left unanswered on purpose; to be settled if a sequel or a longer version needs it.
files.cartes/Oeo9W0AmFU.md:
---
id: Oeo9W0AmFU
type: personnage
title: "The notary"
---
An offstage character. Appointment set for the day after the funeral, for the sale. Had the electricity in the house cut off. Acts as the story’s clock: the night of the well is the last before the signing. In The Morning, the reader calls him at nine to cancel the sale.

files.cartes/U3UZIechv7.md:
---
id: U3UZIechv7
type: evenement
title: "The night of 14 August 2003"
---
A hot night, crickets, a full moon. [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie) falls asleep in her armchair, the only time in forty years. [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK), seven, crosses the yard in striped pyjamas, sandals in hand, head tilted as if listening to a song, and goes down. From the bedroom window, the reader (ten) sees him, hesitates, and goes back to bed, pretending to be asleep.

The gendarmes drag the water for three days. Nothing. Odile circles the 14th in red on the calendar and marks every anniversary for twenty-three years.
files.cartes/UKjsGCEi7z.md:
---
id: UKjsGCEi7z
type: personnage
title: "Fanfan"
---
[@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s dog: yellow, thin, one broken ear. Vanished the first winter after Paul; Odile said he had gone to look for him. Found again in the barn below, the only animal that still moves. He has spent twenty-three years beside [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) and leads the reader to him.
files.cartes/Uu1WZvJKWt.md:
---
id: Uu1WZvJKWt
type: personnage
title: "Marcel"
fiche: {"age":"9 (forever)"}
---
[@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s brother, who went down in her place in 1958, aged nine. Grey wool shorts, side parting, Odile’s grey eyes.

Lives in the kitchen below, where he lays the table (one more plate for the reader, “just in case”). Regrets nothing. Is careful never to ask anyone’s name. Gives the name OURDAS and the rules: you need light, and Paul must recognise the reader.
files.cartes/VRi3ixjgn5.md:
---
id: VRi3ixjgn5
type: groupe
title: "The buyers"
---
A young couple with two children who are to buy [@The Combes farm](cosmos:5xmLViOKEx). Never seen directly: they exist only through the threat they represent. In The Black Water, their little girl leans over the rim; in The Stolen Voice, the false reader sells them the farm and leaves them the key to the padlock. If the pact is not broken, they are the next generation.
files.cartes/W1TAOLcb7U.md:
---
id: W1TAOLcb7U
type: question
title: "Is Paul really Paul?"
---
[@Ourdas](cosmos:nKFYoFi_Cw) speaks with Paul’s voice and has all the memories of the children he keeps. Is the voice in the well Paul, or Ourdas imitating him? The text keeps the doubt alive until the lake: it is the marble or the confession, things Ourdas cannot imitate, that prove the child by the water is the real one.

files.cartes/WNh9vyU3T6.md:
---
id: WNh9vyU3T6
type: lieu
title: "The farm below"
---
The double of [@The Combes farm](cosmos:5xmLViOKEx) beneath the well, reached by the green door and the corridor of walnut roots. The same yard to the centimetre, but silent: instead of a sky, the surface of the well water seen from below, whose reflections make stars. A grey light without shadows, except the reader’s.

The well rises upside down there, up to the sky of water; in it you see the night of 14 August 2003. In the barn, the lost animals and Fanfan the dog. In the kitchen, [@Marcel](cosmos:Uu1WZvJKWt). At the end of a field of grey wheat, the black lake where [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK) waits.

You can make only one detour there.

title: "The niche"
---
A hollow the size of a bread oven in the wall of [@The well](cosmos:ldQZvO2Het), around the thirtieth rung. The children who go down leave their treasure there on their way past: tin soldier, [@Jeanne](cosmos:Cr_QG9CABe)’s ribbon, spinning top, harmonica, porcelain doll’s head, marbles, knucklebones, elder whistle. And, apart, the [@Dragon’s eye](cosmos:3FFhfvLRRn). A small warm hand gently pushes the marble towards the reader.

title: "Odile’s death"
---
Died in her kitchen armchair, in the middle of the night, probably at 3:12. Buried in a fine rain on the morning of the story. With her goes the weight on the lid: “The lid went light,” says [@Marcel](cosmos:Uu1WZvJKWt). This is the inciting incident: [@Ourdas](cosmos:nKFYoFi_Cw)’s debt falls due again.

title: "The iron key"
---
A small blackened key on the board in the workshop, labelled “desk” in [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s hand. Opens the drawer of the walnut bureau the reader once tried to force as a child (the only slap of their life). On the same board, the “well padlock” hook is empty.
files.cartes/iSUsAp4YwJ.md:
---
id: iSUsAp4YwJ
type: objet
title: "Odile’s notebook"
---
A black leather notebook swollen with damp, in the bureau drawer, with [@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie)’s letter to the reader. Full of drawings of the farm upside down under a sky that ripples like water: Odile saw [@The farm below](cosmos:WNh9vyU3T6), or dreamt it. Last page: OURDAS, in capitals, underlined three times.

The letter tells of the pact, of 1958, of the night of 2003, and gives the instruction: “never give it yours”.

files.cartes/ldQZvO2Het.md:
---
id: ldQZvO2Het
type: lieu
title: "The well"
---
At the far end of the yard, it “breathes like a sleeping animal”. White rim, pulley on a beam. Forty rusty iron rungs set into the wall, which nobody had ever seen; the twenty-third is broken. The walls go from mossy brick to a black, glistening stone. A warm wind rises from the bottom, in breaths out: the well is breathing, and you climb down its throat.

A smell of wet stone and forgotten apples. At the bottom, a ledge, black water that reflects nothing but stars, and the green door. Around the thirtieth rung, [@The niche](cosmos:ZPv3kYSJv7).

files.cartes/nKFYoFi_Cw.md:
---
id: nKFYoFi_Cw
type: personnage
title: "Ourdas"
---
“The one who drinks”. Something very old and very thirsty under the farm: deep down, just a thirst that has learnt to speak.

Takes the form of a column of black water in which the faces of the children he has kept slowly turn. Speaks with their voices, and with the voice of anyone who gives him their name.

**Rules:**

-   Never takes anyone by force: he calls, and they go down.
-   Knowing someone’s name gives him their voice and shape (word NAME GIVEN).
-   Saying his name in front of him forces him to listen and breaks the pact, but only with light.
-   Drinks time as well: down below, children don’t grow older.
files.cartes/oRJG-2pebP.md:
---
id: oRJG-2pebP
type: evenement
title: "Marcel goes down (1958)"
---
[@Odile](cosmos:t5FPOkVhie), nine, hears the voice: it is her turn. She is shaking so much she can’t get her clogs on. Her brother [@Marcel](cosmos:Uu1WZvJKWt) goes in her place: “It’s nothing, I’ll be back.” He doesn’t come back. The source of Odile’s guilt, and an exact mirror of the reader’s relationship with [@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK).

files.cartes/t5FPOkVhie.md:
---
id: t5FPOkVhie
type: personnage
title: "Odile"
---
The grandmother. Died in her armchair at 3:12, buried on the day the book begins.

As a child, it was her turn to go down in 1958; her brother Marcel went in her place. Once mistress of the farm, she had the oak lid put on. Fell asleep a single night in forty years: the night Paul went down. Ever since, sat on the lid every night so that Ourdas could not call the other child.

Left a letter and a notebook (Odile’s Letter), with the name OURDAS. Slapped the reader only once, when they tried to open the drawer.

title: "Counting so you’re not afraid"
---
[@Paul](cosmos:8290ZuJdRK)’s rule: “once you have counted something, it can’t scare you any more.” A motif that runs through the whole book: the stairs (thirteen), the rungs (forty, the twenty-third broken), the days scratched on the lid and on the wall, Odile’s crosses on the calendar. In The Black Water, counting becomes the only thing left. In The Morning, the two brothers count together.

Variables in the `choix` blocks:

**Light**

-   `lantern` (true/false) and `flame` (0 to 3): flame = 3 when you take the lantern. −1 climbing down the ladder, −1 if you catch yourself at the broken rung without the rope, −1 examining the marks. +1 refilling the lantern in the barn below.

**Objects**: `rope`, `key` (The Workshop), `notebook` (Odile’s Letter), `marble` (The Niche).

**Words**

-   `ourdas`: Odile’s Letter, The Marks or The Kitchen Below.
-   `twenty_three`: The Silence; lets you step over the broken rung.
-   `memory`: The Upside-Down Well.
-   `recognised`: The Marble or The Confession.
-   `name_given`: saying your name in The Voice; forces The Stolen Voice.

**Endings**: The House, The Black Water, The Stolen Voice, The Exchange, The Name, The Morning (ourdas + recognised + flame > 0).
files.manuscrit/2-UWo3X4YD.md:
At the end of the field of grey wheat there is a lake. Black, smooth, immense. It must be the same water as at the bottom of the well, seen from the other side.

Paul is sitting at the edge.

He hasn’t changed. Of course he hasn’t. The striped pyjamas, the scraped knees, the cowlick on the top of his head that no comb could tame. He is throwing pebbles into the water, one by one. They sink without a sound, without a ripple.

You say his name. Your voice breaks halfway through.

He turns round. He looks you up and down, politely, with the calm suspicion children have for a grown-up they don’t know.

“Who are you? You’re not from the house. At the house there’s Granny, there’s me, and there’s the other one.”

*The other one.* That’s what he called you when he was cross.

“The other one is ten,” he adds. “You’re too old. Too big, I mean. Anyway, you’re too grown-up.” He shrugs and picks up another pebble. “I’m waiting for them. Someone told me they’d come.”

Behind him, the surface of the lake has just moved. For the first time.

```choix
* { marble } [Open your hand and show him the dragon’s eye] -> the_marble
  ~ recognised = true
* { memory } [Kneel down and tell him the truth about that night] -> the_confession
  ~ recognised = true
* [Stay beside him, without a word] -> the_one_who_drinks
```
files.manuscrit/2gJB3nW4Wv.md:
Night falls on the farm. At the far end of the yard, the old well breathes like a sleeping animal.

You haven’t slept here in twenty-three years. This morning you buried your grandmother Odile in a fine rain, in front of a handful of neighbours who stared at you the way people stare at someone back from another country. Tomorrow, the notary. The day after, the buyers. The Combes farm will be sold before the end of the month, and with it the kitchen that smells of wax, the leaning barn, the walnut tree in the yard. And the well.

The well nobody has opened since the summer of 2003. Since Paul.

Your little brother was seven. You were ten. One August morning his bed was empty and his sandals were set side by side on the rim of the well, neat and straight, as if left outside a door. The gendarmes dragged the water for three days. They found nothing. Odile had a lid put on, oak banded with iron, with a padlock the size of a fist, and she never said Paul’s name in front of you again.

Tonight the lid is leaning against the rim. The padlock hangs open.

You stand on the doorstep for a long time. The wind makes the weathervane creak. Somewhere in the dark, water drips, very far down, as regular as a clock.

On the workbench, under the lean-to of the workshop, a lantern is waiting. Someone has filled it with paraffin. The box of matches lies beside it, half open, like an invitation.

```choix
* [Take the lantern] -> taking_the_lantern
  ~ lantern = true
  ~ flame = 3
* [Go into the house first] -> the_kitchen
* [Walk straight to the well, without a light] -> groping_in_the_dark
```
files.manuscrit/48KYjlVuvV.md:
You put the lid back. It is heavier than you remember, and for a second, as you slide it across, you feel something pushing from the other side. You close the padlock. The click echoes across the whole yard.

In the house, you don’t light anything. You climb the stairs counting the steps without meaning to, the way you and Paul used to, to see who would reach the top first. Thirteen. Your childhood bedroom hasn’t changed. The bunk beds. The faded poster. The bolt on the inside, which Odile had fitted the winter after.

You slide the bolt and go to bed. That night you dream of a ladder that never ends.

You wake at twelve minutes past three. You know because the kitchen clock still strikes once at that hour, for no reason, and has for years.

Someone is coming up the stairs. Light steps, bare feet. A small voice counts, very softly: “… eleven… twelve… thirteen.”

Something scratches at the door. Gently. Patiently.

“I know you’re not asleep,” says the voice. “You’re breathing like when you pretended.”

You close your eyes. You breathe slowly. You pretend to be asleep, exactly as you did twenty-three years ago, the night you heard the door downstairs open and didn’t move.

The scratching goes on until dawn.

The next day, at the notary’s, you sign without reading. You will never go back to the Combes. But some nights, at twelve minutes past three, wherever you are, someone is counting steps outside your door.

**THE END.**

```choix
-> END #bad
```
files.manuscrit/6FR8s4v1pK.md:
You bring the light close to the wall.

These are not random marks. They are names. Each carved by a different hand, at a different height, with whatever was to hand: a nail, a belt buckle, a sharp stone.

**ÉTIENNE 1874.** The letters are wide, careful, almost elegant.

**JEANNE 1903.** With a little flower beside it.

**MARCEL 1958.** And below, smaller: *for Odile*.

**PAUL 2003.** The P is backwards, the way he always wrote it when he was in a hurry.

Around the names there are strokes. Thousands of strokes, in groups of five, covering the stone right up to the ceiling. Counted days. Years of days. You try not to imagine how long it takes to fill a wall like that.

And then, between the names, another word keeps coming back. Carved by each child in turn, then crossed out, scribbled over, scratched until it has almost vanished, as if they had learnt it by heart and been afraid of having written it. You trace the letters with your finger.

**OURDAS.**

As you make it out, you feel the well hold its breath.

You stay too long. The light dims.

```choix
* [Push the door at last] -> the_door
```
files.manuscrit/8ozksCJ8rK.md:
It says your name.

In your voice. Your real grown-up voice, the one you hear on voicemail and don’t like. It wears it the way you put on a coat, settling the shoulders.

You open your mouth to answer. Nothing comes out. Not a breath, not a whisper. Your voice is over there, in the standing water, and it goes on talking without you.

“Thank you,” it says. “It’s so much simpler when you give it to us.”

The water shrinks, gathers itself, settles. It takes a shape. Yours. Your height, your way of standing a little crooked, your coat, your shoes. It turns to the ladder and begins to climb, counting the rungs aloud in your voice, cheerfully.

You run after it. The green door shuts in front of you. The latch won’t move.

Paul takes your hand. He says nothing either. He understood before you did, as always.

The next morning, at the notary’s, someone who looks exactly like you signs the deed of sale with a smile. They shake hands with the buyers, a young couple with two children. They tell them the farm is wonderful for little ones, that there is room to play, and a very old well, full of water that never runs dry.

They leave them the key to the padlock.

**THE END.**

```choix
-> END #bad
```
files.manuscrit/98T8dFLkf2.md:
You open your hand.

The dragon’s eye rolls in your palm, and the red spiral flares in the grey light, as if it had been waiting for this moment to wake up.

Paul freezes. The pebble slips from his fingers.

He looks at the marble. Then at you. Then at the marble again. For a long time. You watch something very slow and very complicated cross his face: a child working out a sum too big for him.

“I told you I’d give it to you when you were grown up,” he murmurs.

And he throws himself at you, so hard you nearly fall over backwards. He smells of hay, of wet stone, and beneath all that, faintly, of Odile’s washing powder.

Behind him, the lake rises.

```choix
* [Hold him tight and face it] -> the_one_who_drinks
```
files.manuscrit/9cp8WioqIp.md:
“Take me instead of him.”

You didn’t know you were going to say it. It came out on its own, with a simplicity that surprises you, like a sentence that had been waiting behind your teeth for twenty-three years.

The thing falls silent. All its voices fall silent at once.

“A child of the house,” it says at last, in Jeanne’s voice.

“I was one. I still am. Nobody ever told me I was allowed to stop.”

A long moment passes. Then the standing water bows, very slowly, the way you make a curtsey. Bargain struck.

Paul looks at you without understanding. You lift him up and carry him to the foot of the ladder. He is light, so light. You explain: forty rungs, the twenty-third is broken, you step over it. You tell him to go and knock at the Merciers’, the house at the end of the lane, and to say his name, his real full name. You tell him it will be strange at first. That everything will have changed. That he will have to be brave.

“Braver than you?” he asks.

You laugh. It is the first time in a long while.

You watch him climb. He counts aloud. At twenty-three, he steps over. At forty, his small figure stands out against a circle of sky that is already growing pale. He turns round, waves, and is gone.

In the kitchen below, Marcel has laid a fourth plate. He pulls out the chair for you.

“You’ll see,” he says. “You get used to it. And from down here, you can hear everything.”

High above you, very far away, Paul’s new life is beginning. You will listen to him grow up.

**THE END.**

```choix
-> END
```
files.manuscrit/9oxToWVokE.md:
“Is anyone there?”

Your voice goes down, bounces, and then another voice comes back up. It isn’t yours.

It is a child’s voice. A little hoarse, a little teasing, with a lisp you had forgotten and recognise from the very first word.

“You took ages.”

Your knees hit the stone. You don’t know when your legs gave way. Your hands grip the rim, your face hangs over the void.

“I counted,” the voice goes on. “I counted every single day. On the lid. Granny used to sit on it at night, so I couldn’t get out. But she doesn’t sit there any more.”

A laugh, down below. Bright, delighted.

“Tell me your name. So I’m sure it’s you.”

Something deep in your chest goes stiff. A very old caution, one that doesn’t come from you.

```choix
  ~ name_given = true

```
files.manuscrit/AGwuiASspE.md:
The rim is cold. An iron ladder goes down into the dark, and you can hear water far below.

A ladder. You played around this well a hundred times as a child, and you never saw a ladder. Yet the rungs are there, set into the stone, eaten by rust, as if they had always been there. They sink into a darkness so thick it seems to have a surface.

The air rising from it is warm. It smells of wet stone, and of something else: a sweet, slightly sickly smell, of apples forgotten at the bottom of a basket.

On the inside of the lid, leaning against the rim, the wood is scratched. Hundreds of small marks, close together, regular. They look like the marks you make to count days.

Far below, water drips. Then, between two drops, you think you hear something else. A rubbing sound. A breath being held, exactly like yours.

files.manuscrit/Gy9pofPSPB.md:
You cross the yard without a light. You know this yard by heart. Or you used to.

On the third step your shin hits the trough. On the fifth your hand brushes the bark of the walnut tree, closer than you remember, as if the tree had moved during all these years. The gravel crunches. Then it doesn’t: you are walking on damp, soft earth that has no business being there in a month of drought.

At last your fingers find the rim. The stone is icy and wet, as if it were sweating. Following it with your fingertips, you feel a notch. Then another. A letter, clumsily scratched with the point of a nail or a stone: **P**.

Paul signed everything that way. His drawings, his exercise books, the wood of his bed.

Behind you, over by the workshop, someone laughs.

A short little laugh, muffled in a hand. You turn round. Under the lean-to, on the workbench, the lantern has just lit. By itself. The flame is tiny, blue at its base, and it sways gently, as if someone had just set it down.

No one is there.

```choix
  ~ lantern = true
  ~ flame = 3
* [Stay at the well, in the dark] -> the_well
```

files.manuscrit/HrtEXK9NKI.md:
You are in the farmyard.

The same yard. The walnut tree, the trough, the leaning barn, the house with green shutters, the lean-to of the workshop. Everything is there, in its place, to the centimetre. But nothing makes a sound. Your steps don’t crunch on the gravel. The weathervane turns without creaking.

And there is no sky.

Instead of a sky, very high up, stretches a surface of black water, seen from below. It ripples slowly. The stars you saw earlier when you leant over the water at the bottom are reflections trembling on that surface, thousands of tiny lights that break apart and come together again. You are under the water of the well. You are *under* everything.

The light comes from everywhere and nowhere, the grey light before dawn, and it casts no shadows. Except yours. Yours is the only shadow in the yard, and it seems to be in the way.

In the middle of the yard, exactly where the well should be, a stone column rises towards the sky of water. The well, upside down. Its rim is up there, pressed against the surface.

Somewhere, very far off, a child’s voice is humming a nursery rhyme.

You feel, without knowing how, that this place will not let you see everything. Time, here, is something you drink, and there is little left in your glass. You will only be able to make one detour.

```choix
* [Go into the barn, where there is a smell of warm hay] -> the_barn_below
* [Go towards the kitchen, where a window is lit] -> the_kitchen_below

```
files.manuscrit/IXCnze5N1V.md:
The key turns without resistance, as if the lock had been waiting.

There are only two things in the drawer: a black leather notebook, swollen with damp, and an envelope with your name on it. Odile’s handwriting. You open the envelope.

*If you are reading this, I am dead, and the well is open.*

*I never told you anything because I thought it would die with me. I was wrong about a great many things.*

*Under the farm there is something very old and very thirsty. My great-grandfather made a bargain with it during the great drought: the Combes would never run short of water, and in return, in every generation, a child of the house would go down. Of their own accord. It never takes anyone, you understand. It calls, and you go down.*

*In 1958 it was my turn. I was nine. I heard the voice, I was afraid, and my brother Marcel went in my place. He said to me: “It’s nothing, I’ll be back.”*

*When the farm became mine, I swore no child would ever go down again. I had the lid put on. And then, on the night of 14 August 2003, I fell asleep in the armchair. A single night in forty years.*

*Paul is not dead. Down there, time does not pass. He is still seven. Ever since, every night, I have sat on that lid, so that it could not call you.*

*Its name is in the notebook. It can be bound by saying the name, at the bottom, in front of it. But a name has a price, and you must have light.*

*And above all: never give it yours.*

*I love you. Forgive me for the slap.*

The notebook is full of drawings: the farm, again and again, but upside down, with a sky that ripples like water. On the last page, a single word, in capitals, underlined three times: **OURDAS**.

You slip the notebook into your pocket.

```choix
* { lantern } [Go to the well] -> the_well
* { not lantern } [Go to the well in the dark] -> groping_in_the_dark
* [Burn the letter and go up to bed] -> the_house
```

files.manuscrit/PhtHHaiM37.md:
You climb over the rim. The first rung groans under your weight, then falls silent.

If you have the rope, you tie one end to the pulley beam and the other round your waist. A bowline, the knot Odile taught you for tethering calves. Your hands remember it better than you do.

If you have the lantern, you hook it on your belt. Its light shows the walls up close: first bricks covered in moss, then bare stone, then a black, glistening stone unlike anything you know.

You go down. You count too, without meaning to. Ten. Fifteen. The circle of sky above is no more than a grey coin.

Around the twentieth rung, the wind picks up.

A wind that rises. It comes up from the bottom, warm and steady, like a breath out. Then it stops. Then it comes back. You understand, with a shiver that runs right down to your fingers, that the well is breathing, and that you are climbing down its throat. The draught flattens the lantern’s flame, which takes a long time to stand up again, smaller than before.

Twenty-one. Twenty-two.

Your foot feels for the next rung.

```choix
* { twenty_three } [Step over the twenty-third rung, like Paul] -> the_niche
  ~ flame -= 1
* [Put your foot on the twenty-third rung] -> the_broken_rung
  ~ flame -= 1
```

At the bottom of the well, a door is set into the stone. It is ajar.

The fortieth rung stops a metre above a ledge of dry stone. You jump. The ground is firm, almost warm. At your feet the water begins: black water, perfectly still, so smooth you would take it for a slab of slate. It reflects nothing. Not the lantern, not your face. Only, very far inside it, pale points that look like stars.

The door is made of wood. A real farmhouse door, painted green, with an iron latch and a cat flap cut out at the bottom. It is the door of Odile’s kitchen. You recognise the scrape at hip height that Paul made with his bike.

Through the gap comes a golden light, impossible, the light of a late summer afternoon. And a smell of leek soup. Odile made it on Sundays.

To the right of the door, the wall is covered in carvings: strokes, letters, dates, scratched at a child’s height.

You lay your hand on the wood. It is warm.

files.manuscrit/XmRrwnIWKh.md:
You raise the lantern above your head, and you say:

“**OURDAS**.”

The flame answers the name. It grows all at once, white, immense, and the light bursts through the glass as if someone had just opened a door onto a summer afternoon. The sky of water lights up from below. The thing draws back. For the first time in its very long existence, it has a shadow, and it doesn’t know what to do with it.

“You can’t,” it says, in Paul’s voice.

“Yes,” Paul answers, in his own. “We can.”

He is holding your hand so tight his nails dig into your palm.

The water collapses, comes apart, falls back into the lake in a silent rain. The little lights rise, one by one, set free. Marcel passes very close and whispers in your ear: “Tell her I don’t hold it against her. Tell it to her grave.” Then he goes with the others.

Paul stays.

You carry him on your back to the ladder. You count. He counts with you. At twenty-three, you step over together. Around thirty, as you pass the niche, he tells you to keep the marble after all, “because you’re grown up now, it’s true”.

At forty, the dawn.

The sky is pink above the walnut tree. The birds are starting. You set Paul down on the rim, and he looks at the yard, the house, the workshop, with the seriousness of an inspector.

“Where’s Granny?”

You will have to explain. Everything. The twenty-three years, the grave in the rain, the world that has changed, phones, you growing up without him. It will take a long time. There will be papers, doctors, people who won’t believe you.

None of it matters.

At nine o’clock, you call the notary. You tell him the farm is no longer for sale.

Then you warm some milk in Odile’s kitchen, while Paul, sitting on the rim of the well, puts on his sandals.

**THE END.** *It is the only ending where everyone comes home.*

```choix
-> END #good
```

The kitchen door isn’t locked. It never has been.

You reach for the light switch out of habit. Nothing. The notary had the meter cut off. If you have the lantern, its light slides over the checked oilcloth; if not, it is the moon, through the window, that draws a blue rectangle on the tiles.

Everything is tidy. Too tidy. The dishes are drying on the rack, two bowls, two spoons. The clock above the stove has stopped at twelve minutes past three. The neighbours told you Odile died in her armchair, here, in the middle of the night. They didn’t say what time.

On the table there is a glass of water. Full to the brim. At the bottom, a thin layer of grey sand, and when you come closer, the surface shivers. There is no wind, though. No vibration. The water shivers like skin.

You walk up to the stone column. It rises straight to the sky of water, and at its base, at ground level, there is a round hole. The bottom of the well. Or its mouth. Here, the two are the same thing.

You lean over. You look in.

You see the yard. The real one. From above, as if from a window. It is night, a summer night, hot, full of crickets. The moon lights the walnut tree and the rim. The lid doesn’t exist yet.

A little boy in striped pyjamas crosses the yard. He is carrying his sandals. He walks to the well without hurrying, his head tilted a little, like someone listening to a song.

And up at the window of the children’s bedroom, there is a face. A ten-year-old face, pressed to the glass. Yours.

You see yourself. You see yourself watch Paul set his sandals on the rim, side by side, neat and straight. You see yourself hesitate. You see yourself go back to bed, pull the sheet over your head, and decide very hard that you are asleep.

You had forgotten.

No. That isn’t true. You had *decided* to forget. You decided it that night, and decided it again every day for twenty-three years, so hard that it had become true.

Your chest tightens until it hurts. But in the middle of the pain there is something else, something lighter. Like a door you no longer need to hold shut.

At the far end of the yard, a field of grey wheat stretches down to the water.

```choix
  ~ memory = true
```

files.manuscrit/bVdEUnfHb0.md:
“**OURDAS**.”

The name burns your mouth on the way out, like a mouthful of spirits that are too strong. It costs you something, you can feel it: a little breath, a little warmth, perhaps a few years. You will never know how much.

The thing freezes. All its voices scream at once, then fall silent. The standing water trembles, cracks like ice, and begins to shrink. It is no longer as tall as the barn, but as tall as a man, then a dog, then a puddle. Something very old, very thirsty and very small, deep down. Just a thirst that had learnt to speak.

The little lights come away from it.

One by one, they rise. Étienne. Jeanne. Marcel, who waves to you as he goes by. They float up to the sky of water, pass through it without disturbing it, and disappear.

Paul becomes a light too.

You hold out your arms. But he hasn’t recognised you, or not enough, or not in time, or you no longer had enough light for him to see you. He looks at you for a moment with polite curiosity, the way you look at a kind grown-up outside the school gates, and he goes with the others. You don’t know where. Somewhere you no longer need to count.

You climb back up without him. The ladder is shorter than on the way down. As you step over the rim, dawn is turning the walnut tree pink. You lean over: at the bottom of the well there is no more water. Just a circle of cracked earth, where a tiny blade of grass is already growing.

For the first time in a hundred and fifty years, the Combes well is dry.

You don’t know if you have won. You only know that it is over.

**THE END.** *There is an ending where Paul comes back up.*

```choix
-> END
```
files.manuscrit/cIDbtdWvEc.md:
Around the thirtieth rung, the wall hollows out. A niche, the size of a bread oven, carved into the black stone.

It is full of things.

A tin soldier with chipped paint. A blue satin ribbon, carefully rolled, and on a scrap of yellowed card: *Jeanne*. A wooden spinning top. A rusty harmonica. A porcelain doll’s head with a cracked gaze. Marbles, knucklebones, a whistle cut from an elder branch.

The treasures of the children who came down before you. They left them here on their way past, the way you leave your shoes on a doorstep.

And right at the front, a little apart, a big clear glass marble with a red spiral running through it. The dragon’s eye. Paul’s treasure. He never once lent it to you, not even when you cried for it. He said he would give it to you “when you’re grown up”, and that was the worst thing he could say, because you were already three years older than him.

You reach out.

As your fingers close on the marble, something else brushes them. A small warm hand, which at once draws back into the shadow of the niche. No cry. No fear. Just a gesture, as if to say: go on, take it.

```choix
* [Take the marble and keep climbing down] -> the_bottom
  ~ marble = true
* [Leave it where it is and keep climbing down] -> the_bottom
```
files.manuscrit/ek2Wxixz7m.md:
The lit window is the kitchen’s. You push the green door, for the third time.

A boy is laying the table.

Nine, perhaps ten. Grey wool shorts, socks falling down, a side parting combed with water. He sets the plates out with enormous care: one, two, three, four. He looks up at you, and you recognise Odile’s eyes. The same grey, the same way of frowning before he smiles.

“You must be family,” he says. “You’ve got her nose. I’m Marcel.”

He doesn’t ask your name. You notice he is very careful not to ask it.

“Odile’s dead, isn’t she?” It isn’t really a question. “I felt it. The lid went light.”

He sits down, and while he talks his hands keep smoothing the tablecloth.

“She was frightened that night. She was shaking so much she couldn’t get her clogs on. So I went. I don’t regret it. She had a life, you see? A real one. You, for instance.”

Then he leans towards you and lowers his voice.

“The one who drinks, his name is **OURDAS**. If you say his name in front of him, he has to listen. But you need light, or he’ll drink you before you’ve finished. And Paul…” He hesitates. “Paul won’t follow you if he doesn’t recognise you. You’ve changed a lot. To him, you’re still ten.”

He sets down a fourth spoon, in front of the empty chair.

“That one’s for you. Just in case.”

```choix
* [Leave by the back door Marcel shows you] -> paul
  ~ ourdas = true
```
files.manuscrit/frWW0Ey2HE.md:
The barn door is open. Inside it is warm, and the smell of hay is so strong, so real, that it brings tears to your eyes.

The animals are there.

Not today’s: the farm has had none for a long time. The ones from before. The two white goats that “ran away” the winter you were eight. The old carthorse you only know from the photo in the hallway. Hens, rabbits, a ginger cat. They stand still, upright, eyes open, and their eyes catch the light like glass marbles. They are not sleeping. They are waiting.

Only one moves.

A thin yellow dog with a broken ear gets up from the pile of straw and comes towards you, wagging its tail very gently, as if not sure it is allowed to. Fanfan. Odile’s dog, who disappeared the first winter after Paul. Odile used to say he had gone to look for him.

He puts his nose in your hand. It is cold, but with a living coldness.

Against the wall, on a shelf, a can of paraffin. Full.

Fanfan tugs at your sleeve, towards the back of the barn, where a door you have never seen opens onto a field of grey wheat. He knows where Paul is. He has spent twenty-three years beside him.

```choix
* { lantern } [Fill the lantern, then follow the dog] -> paul
  ~ flame += 1
* [Follow the dog] -> paul
```

Your foot comes down on the twenty-third rung.

It gives way.

The rotten iron snaps like a dry branch, and your body tips backwards into the void, all your weight at once. Time stretches. You have time to see the piece of iron spin beneath you, to hear it fall, for a long time, far too long, before the splash.

Higher up, you think you hear someone stifle a cry. Or a laugh.

files.manuscrit/h_AHsNP5rQ.md:
You kneel in front of him, so that your eyes are level.

And you tell him the truth. That you saw him cross the yard that night. That you saw him put his sandals on the rim. That you didn’t move. That you pulled the sheet over your head and pretended to be asleep, so hard you ended up believing it. That you have regretted it every day since, even the days you didn’t remember.

Your voice shakes. You don’t stop.

Paul stares at you. He says nothing for a long while. Then he wrinkles his nose, exactly like before, when he had just caught you out.

“I knew you were pretending. You breathe too loud.”

He slips his hand into yours. It is small and cold, and it doesn’t let go.

Behind him, the lake rises.

```choix
* [Get up and face it, his hand in yours] -> the_one_who_drinks
```
files.manuscrit/kElYuabMSz.md:
The lake rises.

Not a wave: a shape. The water of the lake climbs and stands upright, as tall as the barn, with no fixed outline, and inside it the little lights you took for stars turn slowly. Up close, you see what they are: faces. Tiny, pale, asleep. Étienne. Jeanne. Marcel. And others, many others, older than the farm.

When the thing speaks, it speaks with their voices. All at once, then one, then another, the way you look for the right tool on a wall.

“The old woman is dead,” it says in Jeanne’s voice. “She used to sit on me. Forty years.” In Marcel’s voice: “It was a long time.” And then, in Paul’s voice, exactly Paul’s voice, which is the worst of all: “Now it’s your turn. The debt is due. It needs a child of the house.”

Paul presses against your leg. Or against nothing, if he hasn’t recognised you.

The air turns dry, so dry your lips split. You understand that it is already drinking you, a little, to get the taste.

files.manuscrit/lmMHad2fZS.md:
You say nothing. You hold your breath and listen.

For a long time there is only the water. One drop. Another. Then, far below, a sound of metal, a faint ring, like a fingernail against a rung. And a child’s voice, whispering to itself:

“… nineteen… twenty… twenty-one… twenty-two…”

A pause.

“Twenty-three, careful, it’s broken, step over it… twenty-four…”

You know this game. Paul counted everything. Stairs, cobblestones, cows in the field, the seconds between lightning and thunder. He said that once you have counted something, it can’t scare you any more.

The voice goes on, flat, all the way to “forty”. Then a small splash, a pebble dropped in. A laugh.

And suddenly, very close, as if the mouth were just below the rim:

“I know you’re there. You’re breathing like when you pretended to be asleep.”

You jerk back. Your heart pounds. You have never told anyone about that.

```choix
* [Climb down the ladder] -> the_ladder
  ~ twenty_three = true
* [Put the lid back and go inside] -> the_house
```
files.manuscrit/r0jxMMCItj.md:
The water is cold. Not cold like a river in winter: cold like the absence of anything at all.

It closes over you without a sound. You don’t sink, you descend, gently, and there is no more up or down. Your light, if you had one, goes out without a hiss. The dark is complete, and yet you can see. You see the pale little lights turning around you. They come closer, curious, and one of them has the face of a boy in short trousers, shaking his head sadly.

You try to scream. What comes out of your mouth isn’t a scream. It is counting. *One. Two. Three.* You count, because once you have counted something, it can’t scare you any more.

You count for a very long time.

Then one day, or one night, there is no longer any difference, a light appears high above you. A grey circle. A small head leaning over the rim. A little girl, this time. The buyers had two children.

“Is anyone there?” she asks.

And you hear yourself answer, in a voice that is no longer quite yours, a soft voice, patient, affectionate:

“You took ages.”

**THE END.**

files.manuscrit/s29K0qfCKt.md:
The workshop smells of linseed oil and sawdust. The lantern makes the shadows of the tools hanging from the beams dance, and for a moment the whole workshop seems to move with you.

On the big nail by the door, a hemp rope is coiled in a crown. Fifteen metres at least, as thick as a thumb. One end has been cut clean, recently: the fibres are still blond.

Above the workbench, a key board. Each key has a pencilled label in Odile’s slanting hand: *barn*, *cellar*, *henhouse*, *well padlock*. The padlock hook is empty. Next to it hangs a small blackened iron key, labelled *desk*.

And then there is the calendar.

A post office calendar from 2003, pinned to the wall, never replaced. August is still showing. The 14th is circled in red. But below it, on a sheet of brown paper taped on, Odile kept going: *2004, 2005, 2006…* A column of years down to this one. A small cross beside each. The last one dated last summer.

Under the column, one sentence, in a hand that was already shaking:

*As long as I sit on it, he can’t come up.*

files.manuscrit/vGWKjODaWa.md:
The door opens without a creak. The golden light you saw through the gap has gone: behind it there is only a narrow corridor with a low ceiling, whose walls are made of roots.

Enormous roots, knotted, laced together like fingers. You know them by their bitter smell, the smell of walnut husks that stains your hands for days. The walnut tree in the yard. You are walking under it, or rather inside it, through what it has been hiding underground for two hundred years.

The roots whisper.

Not in words, at first. A rustle, like silk being unfolded. Then, as you go on, you make out first names. *Étienne. Jeanne. Marcel.* Repeated softly, tenderly, the way you call a child in for supper.

And then, once, barely audible: your own name.

You stop. The whispering stops too. It is waiting to see whether you will answer.

You don’t answer. You walk on.

At the end of the corridor stands a second door. Green, with an iron latch, a cat flap and a scrape at hip height. Exactly the same as the first. You have a very clear feeling of having passed through something, but you couldn’t say whether it was a corridor, a mirror, or the years.

```choix
* [Lift the latch] -> the_yard_below
```
